etymology_text:
From Proto-Semitic *šinn- (“tooth”), the source of שן. The association of "tooth" with this letter was the result of folk etymology and based on the corresponding Phoenician letter, 𐤔 (š), having a shape resembling a tooth. The letter originally depicted a composite bow, which usually has the tips curving away from the archer when unstrung.
Related to Classical Syriac ܫ, Arabic ش (š), Phoenician 𐤔 (š), Russian ш (š), Aramaic ܫ. More at Shin.

examples.text: שׁ is shin (with the shin dot above the right-hand side of the letter), representing /ʃ/
שׂ is sin (with the sin dot above the left-hand side of the letter), representing /s/

glosses: Shin or sin: the twenty-first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, after ר and before ת.
